  • According to recent reports, the future of the ministry of culture has been a subject of debate in the lead-up to the election.
  • In a recent development, the prospect of such a transfer has raised concerns over censorship, particularly in the light of a wave of cancelled art festivals and plays in PP-Vox-led regions since the 2023 regional elections.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that spain’s snap elections, due to take place on 29 November, have left several long-awaited newly introduced measures and legislation for art and culture hanging in the balance. These include regulations on AI, intellectual property and artist welfare. With a coalition between the conservative Partido Popular (PP) and the far-right Vox party looking increasingly likely, here is what the vote could mean for the country’s art and culture sector.

According to recent reports, the future of the ministry of culture has been a subject of debate in the lead-up to the election. PP has argued in favour of maintaining it, albeit merged with other portfolios, but Vox will only support the ministry’s existence if cultural powers presently held by Spain’s autonomous communities are transferred to the central government.

In a recent development, the prospect of such a transfer has raised concerns over censorship, particularly in the light of a wave of cancelled art festivals and plays in PP-Vox-led regions since the 2023 regional elections. At a party meeting on 22 November, Vox’s secretary general, Ignacio Garriga, stated that they will support cultural professionals who “create quality national products” and “highlight the value of the country's culture”.

Even if the ministry of culture continues, the sector expects budget cuts under a PP-Vox coalition. The PP has pledged to promptly pass a latest patronage law with tax and legal incentives to encourage private businesses and individuals to fund cultural projects, arguing that healthcare and defence spending will leave culture underfunded by the state. The PP's proposals for culture also include auditing working conditions, exhibition standards and security protocols across national museums.

It has been revealed that the Status of the Artist bill, a welfare package designed to improve working conditions of those in the cultural sector, will enter into force in 2027 regardless of the election results, after being approved by the Council of Ministers in July. However, the inclusion of visual artists—who, unlike other types of artists, were entirely left out of the bill and continue to face prohibitive self-employment quotas—remains up in the air.

Earlier this year, the Union of Contemporary Artists of Spain launched a campaign to push for their inclusion with the support of the ministry of culture, but the decision stalled in the ministries of social security and finance. Gloria Reguero, the president of the union, notes that they have been waiting since 2018 for painters, sculptors and photographers to be recognised as artists. “Just when it seemed we were going to start negotiating our terms, the elections came along, and with them, another setback,” she tells The Art Newspaper.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, a separate draft bill regulating the use of generative AI in the arts is not getting off the ground at all. The legislation was put out for public consultation in late September and it marked the government’s third attempt to regulate AI in the arts following two failed royal decrees. The draft bill sought to prohibit the use of generative AI to exploit an artist’s image, voice or work without their express consent and specific remuneration and, like the Status of the Artist, it left out the visual arts.

Sources indicate that both PP and Vox have strongly opposed aims by Ernest Urtasun, the current Spanish culture minister, to review state museum collections—specifically the Museum of the Americas and the National Museum of Anthropology—to “move past a colonial framework”. When the initiative was first announced in early 2024, the PP dismissed the push for decolonisation, in a statement, as “a false debate, imposed and manufactured to create division among Spaniards”.

In November 2025, the ministry formally presented a €13.6m project to overhaul the permanent exhibitions and narratives of both institutions through an “anti-racist and gender perspective”.

Recent findings suggest that ahead of the elections, the project has reached different stages: while the National Museum of Anthropology has already moved through its public tendering process for the remodelling of its permanent exhibition, the Museum of the Americas remains at an earlier stage, with major works still pending. If a new government takes office, the initiative’s long-term completion, scheduled for 2028, faces significant uncertainty—with a risk that yet-to-be-contracted tenders may be halted or that curatorial direction may be revised. A spokesperson for the Museum of the Americas declined to respond to The Art Newspaper's request for comment, “especially now that we’re on the eve of the elections and everything is so uncertain”, they say.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly introduced photography book offers a glimpse into Europe’s underground rave culture at the turn of the millennium, documenting the free-party movement through the eyes of two photographers who were part of the scene.

Never Alone 1997–2004: Raving in Europe, by Cheyenne Clementi and Valentina Morandi, features 160 original analog photographs made between 1997 and 2004. The images document a period when free parties were spreading across Europe, offering an alternative to mainstream society through music, community, and a shared rejection of conventional lifestyles.

Sources indicate that rather than documenting the movement as outsiders, Clementi and Morandi were active participants in the culture. Their photographs provide a firsthand account of a counterculture built around emotion, affection, and togetherness, at a time when music and personal connections — rather than social media and mass communication — brought people together.

The book spans 196 black-and-white pages and brings together previously unseen photographs that capture the atmosphere and values of the era. Its accompanying text is written by Tobia D’Onofrio, author of Rave Latest World, who explores the history and significance of the European free-party movement.

“Rave was born as a disappearing ritual in which the art of invisibility was practiced, and parties were temporarily autonomous and free zones that appeared and disappeared into thin air within a few hours,” claims D’Onofrio.

Recent findings suggest that “1997–2004 can therefore be considered the golden age of the so-called illegal free parties and of rave culture. It was the moment of the phenomenon’s expansion across Europe… the rave scene had been criminalized to the point that in 1994 the Criminal Justice Act in England outlawed free parties. At that point, the energies shifted to the rest of Europe, and Italy immediately became the scene of legendary parties.”.

In a recent development, the book examines how rave culture developed into more than a musical movement. It represented a rejection of conventional working and social structures, embracing communal living, constant movement, and a different relationship with time and space. Free parties became meeting places for people united by anarchic sensibilities and a desire to escape everyday routines.

Recent findings suggest that clementi and Morandi both attended the same high school in Milan before pursuing separate careers. Despite taking different paths, both remained dedicated to photography, eventually bringing their shared rave-scene experiences together in Never Alone.

The book is available online and through specialist bookstores.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Koto's De-extinction brand identity turns compostable packaging into a protest, with loud dinosaurs, acid green and hot pink.

Industry observers note that the dinosaurs are back as warnings. Koto draws them in thick black outlines and fills them with acid green and hot pink, then sets them loose across kraft cups, stickered boxes and poster walls. The palette is deliberately loud: acid green, hot magenta, black and off-white, with the brown of the compostable board keeping the whole system grounded. The posters shout in stacked capitals, Sweet packaging without the sour aftertaste and Re-package your future, while the product photography drops the cups into a lush jungle world of flowers, rock and mist. Koto calls the idea Once Upon A Time, and even created the De-extinction name, a reminder that extinction is real unless we act.

It has been revealed that the type does the shouting. A heavy grotesque runs at poster scale in tight stacked lines, with single words reversed out of black bars: FEED and NOURISH picked out in white on black, PLANET highlighted in pink. The de-extinction wordmark stays small and lowercase beside a round dino mark, letting the headlines carry the volume. The same bluntness holds where the system has to be practical: a catalog page lists cold cup sizes in a plain table under a giant COLD CUPS header, with a small dino doodle at the foot.

Industry observers note that the packaging is the proof. Kraft cups carry the small dino mark, boxes arrive covered in dino stickers, and a paper bag sits in the jungle photography with the same mark. Nothing is coated in gloss: the board stays brown, the print stays flat, and the dinosaurs do the talking. Koto took its cue from protest culture and global movements, building the brand to provoke action rather than nod at it, and the identity runs the same way across packaging, posters and communications. The approach landed: the identity helped the young organization stand out with key customers, including meetings with Sweetgreen.

See more from Koto on the De-extinction project page.

Estudio A-G uses colour to update 1960s book-lined house in Mexico City

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Leandro Bulzzano, Ricardo Letona.
  • Local studio Estudio A-G has foregrounded a sculptural timber structural element while implementing bold colours for the renovation of a 1960s house in Mexico City.
  • Originally built in 1962 by Jaime Ortiz Monasterio, Casa Magnolia is located in the residential neighbourhood of San Ángel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Leandro Bulzzano, Ricardo Letona.

Local studio Estudio A-G has foregrounded a sculptural timber structural element while implementing bold colours for the renovation of a 1960s house in Mexico City.

Originally built in 1962 by Jaime Ortiz Monasterio, Casa Magnolia is located in the residential neighbourhood of San Ángel.

Industry observers note that monasterio designed the home as a domestic library for his brother, who was an avid reader and book collector. Over the decades, the house was renovated multiple times, obscuring the home’s original character.

In 2025, Andrés Gutiérrez, head of Estudio A-G, was commissioned to reinterpret the interior of the 275-square-metre residence for new inhabitants, preserving the architectural qualities that made the original design unique.

“The restoration was extremely respectful of the house’s original architecture, but we never wanted the result to feel nostalgic,” Gutiérrez told Dezeen.

“Quite the opposite – once restored, the house needed to feel completely latest, fresh and contemporary, which was exactly what the clients were looking for.”.

It has been revealed that completed in February 2026, the design uses colour to achieve the transformation, bringing fresh energy to the original architecture without competing with it. The studio aimed to have the house be recognisably Mexican without falling into tropes.

“I wanted the house to feel unmistakably Mexican, but without relying on folklore or the usual clichés associated with ‘Mexican interiors’.” he said.

“I was much more interested in expressing that identity through materials, craftsmanship, colour and contemporary Mexican design.”.

At the centre of the house, a dark-toned timber structure rises through a series of split levels like a sculptural tree connecting the entrance hall, living room, dining room, study and reading areas before unfolding into a double-height ceiling.

“More than a structural element, it serves as a spatial anchor, establishing continuity throughout the interior and reinforcing the vertical dimension of the house,” Gutiérrez said, explaining that wood acts as a warm, unifying element throughout the house.

In a recent development, the studio restored and reintegrated the original wood flooring, ceiling finishes and structural elements. It also reinstalled most of the original wooden bookshelves that had been dismantled and stored.

“Overall, the intervention focused on restoring the elements that were worth preserving while introducing the necessary contemporary updates to make the house fully functional for the way its new owners live today,” he said.

The studio replaced some window frames and all the glass, updated the lighting and electrical systems and rebuilt the bathrooms and kitchen.

However, one of the most significant interventions were the colour blocks and new materials included in the space.

“Colour plays a central role in the project,” Gutiérrez said, calling out soft blue walls that are a backdrop for deep plum sofas, moss green dining chairs, lilac rugs, green serpentine stone and terracotta-toned marble.

“Rather than acting as decoration, colour is used as an architectural tool to organise space, establish hierarchy, and shape atmosphere.”.

He also designed custom furniture that pairs with historic pieces – like Antonio Attolini’s 1969 armchairs – and contemporary Mexican art. Works by Cecilia Barreto, Francisco Muñoz, Jorge Rosano, Daniel Berman and Adriana Silva embed culture into everyday life.

Previously, Estudio A-G designed a rooftop bar as a “matriarchal universe,” complete with crocodile-shaped furniture and shrine-like water, for a boutique hotel in a former Spanish colonial manor house in San Miguel de Allende.

A student photographer who lost his right eye after he was allegedly struck by a projectile fired by a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) agent while covering a “No Kings” protest is suing the federal government.

Warning: The following photos contain content that some may find upsetting.

Tucker Collins, an 18-year-old freshman at the University of Southern California (USC), was left partially blind after photographing demonstrators in downtown Los Angeles on the afternoon of March 28. Collins was allegedly photographing a confrontation between protesters and federal agents when he was allegedly hit by a less-lethal projectile.

Sources indicate that footage highlights Collins taking pictures of demonstrators outside a federal facility before suddenly falling to his knees as a crowd-control projectile reportedly struck him in the right eye, fracturing bones in his eye socket. Collins was taken to a hospital, where he underwent two and a half hours of surgery in an attempt to save the eye. The injury was too severe, and the eye was surgically removed.

Collins sued the federal government on Monday, alleging that law enforcement officers used excessive force and violated his civil rights. According to a report by The Upcoming York Times, his attorneys allege that Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officers “assaulted” and “used unjustified force against him” as he photographed the protest.

The lawsuit seeks various damages from the federal government, “including past and future medical expenses, prosthetic and ophthalmologic care, educational expenses, and loss of earning capacity.”.

Collins’s attorney, V. James DeSimone, and his family are also demanding criminal charges against the officer responsible for shooting him. They argue that the officer’s actions violated California law governing the use of projectile launchers by law enforcement.

The lawsuit also details how Collins’s injuries have limited his ability to pursue activities he once enjoyed, including photography. Collins indicates he is no longer able to safely photograph public events similar to the protest where he was injured. DeSimone also condemned the lack of criminal accountability in the wake of the shooting.

Recent findings suggest that “It is deeply disturbing that the maiming of Tucker Collins, resulting in the loss of his eye, was widely reported and captured on video and, yet, there is no law enforcement response, to date, on the Federal, State or Local level to prosecute the offending officer for his crime,” DeSimone indicates in a statement. “Once again, it is left to civil rights attorneys to attempt to achieve some semblance of justice for the permanent and irreversible harm caused to this courageous young man.”.

NASA astronaut Anil Menon captured a spectacular video of a moonset yesterday (Tuesday) from onboard the International Space Station.

The mesmerizing footage demonstrates Earth’s natural satellite melting into the atmosphere as it disappears behind Earth.

“This is a real-time video of a moonset today from the space station cupola on a [Nikon] Z9 and 400mm lens,” Menon writes on his Instagram page.

A post shared by Anil | Astronaut Space Doctor (@astro_anil).

Menon also shared a series of photos, which he specifically states contain “no edits or alterations.” Menon, a colonel in the United States Space Force, flew to the ISS in July 2026 as part of Expedition 75, for which he is a flight engineer.

A post shared by Anil | Astronaut Space Doctor (@astro_anil).

Not too long after he joined the floating space station, Menon snapped a mind-boggling photo of a super typhoon brooding above the Pacific Ocean — on his iPhone.

Just like the moonset photos, Menon took the typhoon photo from the space station’s cupola, a dome-shaped panoramic observatory module featuring six circumferential windows and a central nadir viewing window.

According to recent reports, the cupola is where so much of the fantastic photography is made on the ISS. Menon recently shared a behind-the-scenes video showing how astronauts set up shots inside the seven-sided window.

A post shared by Anil | Astronaut Space Doctor (@astro_anil).

“Welcome to the cupola,” says Menon. “This is a camera. That’s planet Earth. Here are our seven windows that we can look down at Earth with, and I’m going to take this camera and set it up for a night shot.”.

Industry observers note that during the video, day is slowly turning to night. “Because we’re going to take a long exposure, we need to keep it stable, so we’ll set the camera up in the window, tighten it up so it’s stable, and we can put in our settings,” Menon explains.

In a recent development, “But a lot of light is going to leak in from the sides because there’s a lot of LEDs around; there are power strips and things that can get in, so we put this shroud over the camera. That way, the lens is facing out at planet Earth, and it is hidden from the light.”.

  • Recent findings suggest that jehovah’s Witnesses were persecuted by the Nazis for their religious beliefs, particularly their refusal to serve in the military, pledge allegiance to Adolf Hitler, or participate in Nazi organizations.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The German government has agreed to hand over an extensive photo archive to the Jehovah’s Witnesses that documents the persecution of a pacifist Christian family under the Nazi regime.

Recent findings suggest that jehovah’s Witnesses were persecuted by the Nazis for their religious beliefs, particularly their refusal to serve in the military, pledge allegiance to Adolf Hitler, or participate in Nazi organizations. An estimated 4,500 Jehovah’s Witnesses were sent to concentration camps.

According to a report by The Latest York Times, among those persecuted were Franz and Hilda Kusserow and their 11 children, who lived in Bad Lippspringe, a town in the German state of North Rhine-Westphalia. Two of the couple’s sons were executed after refusing military service because of their religious beliefs. The three youngest children were taken from their family and placed in a Nazi training school, where they were prohibited from contacting their relatives. Both parents and their remaining children were sentenced to prison terms.

One of their daughters Annemarie Kusserow was arrested by the Gestapo in October 1944 and remained a prisoner until May 25, 1945, after the war in Europe had ended. Over the following decades, Annemarie gathered and preserved a collection of more than 1,000 photographs, documents, drawings, letters, and reports documenting her family’s experiences.

It has been revealed that in her 2005 will, Annemarie bequeathed the entire photo archive to the German headquarters of the Jehovah’s Witnesses. However, her brother Hans Werner Kusserow, to whom she had loaned the collection for research purposes, sold it to the Bundeswehr Military History Museum in Dresden, Germany, in 2009. The archive has remained in the German museum’s possession ever since.

According to the Jehovah’s Witnesses’ official website, the sale of the photo collection to a military museum was “especially troubling” given that two of Annemarie’s brothers had lost their lives because of their pacifist beliefs. The organization notes the sale of the archive “resulted in years of legal battles.”.

The Jehovah’s Witnesses filed a lawsuit to recover the archive from the Bundeswehr Military History Museum, which is operated by the German armed forces. On November 19, the museum and the religious organization reached an “amicable agreement” under which the collection will be handed over to the Jehovah’s Witnesses. Both parties have agreed to keep the terms of the settlement confidential.

According to The Latest York Times, Sebastian Stock, a spokesman for the religious organization in Germany, notes that once the transfer is complete, the “Jehovah’s Witnesses will develop and present a concept for making the archive accessible for further academic research.”.

In addition to digitizing the archive and making it available to scholars, the Jehovah’s Witnesses plan to display some of the documents in a upcoming exhibition examining the history of the religious group in Central Europe.

  • Sources indicate that in previous editions of the Biennale, an international jury has selected the artist and national pavilion to receive the prizes, traditionally known as Golden Lions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Venice Biennale has named the American artist Nick Cave and India’s national pavilion as the winners of its top art prizes this year, following a controversy that saw the competition’s jury resign and several artists and pavilions withdraw from the running.

Sources indicate that in previous editions of the Biennale, an international jury has selected the artist and national pavilion to receive the prizes, traditionally known as Golden Lions. This year, however, the awards were renamed Visitors’ Lions and awarded on the basis of votes cast by visitors to the exhibition.

In a recent development, the new voting system was introduced following a dispute over the inclusion of Russia and Israel in the 2026 Biennale. In a statement in April, the five-person jury announced that it would not award prizes to national pavilions or artists from countries whose leaders were charged with crimes against humanity by the International Criminal Court (ICC).

The International Criminal Court had issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin, Russia's president, in 2023, and for Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's prime minister, the following year.

The jurors resigned days later, saying they were doing so “in acknowledgement” of their previous statement.

Dozens of artists then ruled themselves out of the contest in solidarity with the jury, though they remained on the ballot. The Biennale clarified that votes for withdrawn entries would not be considered.

It is unclear whether Cave and the India pavilion received the most votes of all entries on the ballot, including withdrawn entries. The Biennale declined to provide The Art Newspaper with a breakdown of the results.

“The Venice Biennale does not publish rankings or detailed voting results, as the regulations do not provide for this,” a Biennale spokesperson tells The Art Newspaper. “This applies to the Visitors’ Lions, just as it has always applied to the decisions of the international juries.”.

According to recent reports, cave is best known for work that combines fashion, sculpture and performance. His exhibition at Venice’s Arsenal includes seven works, among them Amalgam (Origin) (2024), a monumental bronze sculpture of a figure with branches growing out of its body and birds nestling among twigs. Each of the seven works address a stage of grief.

Sources indicate that "On the eve of Thanksgiving, I feel an even deeper sense of gratitude, for the friendship that bound me with Koyo Kouoh, and for the fact that she decided to include my work in the In Minor Keys exhibition," Cave stated in a statement. "This project is a synthesis of my wider artistic research: it recognises the history of violence and oppression that Black people have endured and continue to endure in the United States, and it pays tribute to the beauty created by that very community, expressing the possibility of growth towards a different future.".

India's exhibition, titled Geographies of Distance, features works by five artists including clay sculptures, dried flowers and plants hung from the ceiling, and a demolished family home reconstructed in white thread. Curated by Amin Jaffer, the exhibition reflects on the rapid expansion of cities in India, according to the Biennale's website.

Installation view of India’s pavilion at the 2026 Venice Biennale, Geographies of Distance: remembering home.

Industry observers note that photo: Jacopo Salvi. Courtesy of La Biennale di Venezia.

On Wednesday, when this year's winners were announced, Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, the Biennale’s president, praised the new voting system.

He said in a statement: “The public of the Exhibition embraced this recognition—the Visitors’ Award—as an opportunity to bring Pablo Picasso’s practice to life: a painting only comes to life through the person who looks at it".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography courtesy of Mason & Fifth.

Design studio Holloway Li has collaborated with architecture practice Latest-works to conceive the interiors of this London apartment hotel, incorporating circular features meant to stand the test of time.

Mason & Fifth guesthouses are composed of fully furnished private apartments where guests have the flexibility of staying anywhere from one night to several months at a time.

The organization has three sites across London, with one in Primrose Hill, another in Westbourne Park, and now Belsize Park.

The Belsize Park location occupies Ornan Court, a 19th-century mansion block that once formed part of the Ivy Bank residential estate.

Architecture practice Fresh-works adapted the building for hospitality use, establishing a series of communal spaces at ground level that could serve as a social hub for guests.

At its heart is a large shared kitchen, centred by a chunky tiled breakfast island, followed by a lounge area with intimate groupings of timber-frame chairs and two khaki-coloured sofas, complementing the glossy green fireplace.

In a recent development, just off this space is a cosy snug that’s been painted a warm ochre hue. It’s separated from the lounge by a custom-made curtain that design studio House of Quinn made from earth-toned fabric offcuts.

Sources indicate that holloway Li is behind the design of the interiors. Instead of doing a through-and-through overhaul, the studio instead aimed to develop a “circular economy aesthetic that felt warm, domestic and low-impact”.

“That ambition aligned with Mason & Fifth’s own sustainability agenda and allowed us to explore how historic buildings like this can be retrofitted in imaginative and progressive ways,” said the studio’s creative director Alex Holloway.

In each of the guesthouse’s 56 apartments, the bedrooms are furnished with demountable wardrobes in lieu of fitted joinery.

The wardrobes are made up of lightweight timber parts fixed together with metal brackets rather than glue so that, if necessary, they can be unassembled, flat packed, and re-built elsewhere.

Holloway Li worked with Marble Collective to create countertops and splashbacks for the apartment kitchens; all are crafted from limestone that’s been rejected from quarries because of inconsistencies.

The top edge of the splashbacks has been left slightly craggy and unfinished, further celebrating the stone’s natural flaws.

Almost all of the walls throughout the guesthouse have been simply rendered with multi-finish plaster, and any surface imperfections have been left on show.

“In many cases, the most sustainable decision is restraint,” explained Holloway Li’s senior designer Carrie Coningsby.

“Drawing on principles akin to kintsugi and spolia, the approach celebrates intervention rather than concealing it, embedding repair into the visual language of the space,” she added, referencing historic practices focused on reuse and repair instead of replacement.

Mason & Fifth Belsize Park was shortlisted in the sustainable interior category of this year’s Dezeen Awards.

Other projects in the running included the winning Cloudhaus Hotel by RooMoo, which is outfitted with materials salvaged from abandoned mountain cabins, and the London Coffee Factory by Steve Jensen Design, which is structured around a reclaimed timber framework.

Photography courtesy of Mason & Fifth.

Most estate planning advice assumes you will work until 60-65, accumulate wealth gradually, and have employer-provided benefits until Medicare kicks in. The FIRE path breaks every one of those assumptions. You may stop working at 35, 40, or 50 — meaning your estate plan must cover a potentially 40 to 50-year retirement, not the 20 to 25-year retirement conventional planning addresses.

This extended timeline creates unique vulnerabilities:.

The SECURE Act fundamentally changed how inherited retirement accounts work, and this change matters enormously for FIRE households that have built large tax-advantaged portfolios.

Before the SECURE Act, non-spouse beneficiaries could "stretch" inherited IRA distributions over their own lifetime, allowing decades of tax-deferred growth. Now, most non-spouse beneficiaries must withdraw the entire inherited IRA balance within 10 years of the original owner's death. For a beneficiary in their peak earning years, this compressed timeline can push them into the 32% or 37% tax bracket on every distribution.

The FIRE advantage: Early retirees have years — sometimes decades — of lower taxable income between leaving work and taking Social Security or required minimum distributions. This creates a golden window for Roth conversions that no conventional retiree has.

Sources indicate that A married couple who retires at 40 with $1.5 million in a traditional 401(k) and a $500,000 Roth IRA could systematically convert $80,000 to $100,000 per year from the traditional to the Roth, staying within the 22% bracket. Over 15 years, they convert $1.2 million to $1.5 million at a known, relatively low tax rate. Their heirs then inherit a Roth IRA that is completely tax-free — even under the SECURE Act's 10-year distribution rule.

Industry observers note that without conversions, those heirs would owe ordinary income tax on every dollar withdrawn from the inherited traditional IRA, potentially at 32% or higher if they are working professionals during their peak earning years. The tax savings for heirs can easily exceed $200,000 to $400,000 on a $1.5 million inherited traditional IRA.

It has been revealed that key Roth inheritance rule: Inherited Roth IRAs are still subject to the 10-year distribution rule, but the distributions are tax-free. The 10-year clock starts the year after the original owner's death.

If you have reached FI with $500,000 or more in assets, a revocable living trust adds significant value through probate avoidance and incapacity protection.

Industry observers note that most non-spouse beneficiaries must now withdraw the entire inherited IRA or 401(k) within 10 years of the original owner's death. This compressed timeline can push heirs into high tax brackets. Roth conversions during your lifetime eliminate this tax burden because inherited Roth IRA distributions are tax-free.

For most early retirees, transferring your primary residence to a revocable living trust makes sense. It avoids probate on the home, enables seamless management if you become incapacitated, and does not affect your mortgage, property tax, or homestead exemption in most states. Consult your estate attorney about your state's specific rules.

Industry observers note that umbrella insurance provides liability coverage above the limits of your auto and homeowners policies. A $1 million umbrella policy typically costs $200 to $300 per year and protects against lawsuits, car accident judgments, and liability claims that exceed your underlying policy limits. For FIRE households with significant assets, it is one of the most cost-effective forms of protection available.

This is significantly cheaper than the 32% or 37% rate your heirs might pay on inherited traditional IRA distributions.

Review your estate blueprint every three years at minimum and immediately after any major life event: marriage, divorce, birth of a child, death of a beneficiary, significant change in net worth, or a move to a new state. Early retirees have a longer planning horizon, making regular updates even more important than for conventional retirees.

In a recent development, estate planning for early retirees is not a modified version of conventional retirement planning — it is a fundamentally different discipline. You face a longer incapacity window, a bigger healthcare gap, more exposure to tax law changes, and decades of asset protection needs. The FIRE community excels at building wealth through savings rate optimization and investment discipline. Apply that same rigor to your estate strategy: execute foundational documents before leaving your job, optimize beneficiary designations for the SECURE Act, pursue Roth conversions during low-income years, and protect your assets with umbrella insurance and trust structures. The wealth you built deserves a plan that survives as long as your retirement.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Brightin Star first unveiled its newly introduced APO 35mm f/1.7 ASPH.
  • The Brightin Star 35mm f/1.7 APO ASPH.
  • In a recent development, although rangefinder-coupled with close focusing down to 0.7 meters (2.3 feet), the lens can focus as close as 0.3 meters (0.98 feet) when used in live view or adapted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brightin Star first unveiled its newly introduced APO 35mm f/1.7 ASPH. lens for Leica M-Mount cameras at CP+ in February and then launched it on Kickstarter in August. As of today, it’s available to everyone, and it’s still as handsome as ever.

The Brightin Star 35mm f/1.7 APO ASPH. is a full-frame, manual-focus lens with a native Leica M-Mount design. However, as evidenced by the fact that Brightin Star offers it in kits with E, Z, RF, X, L, and even GFX adapters, it’s easy to adapt to other camera systems. Although Brightin Star does not state the lens’s exact image circle when used with its GFX adapter, the company indicates it covers the 44 x 33-millimeter sensor inside GFX system medium-format mirrorless cameras.

In a recent development, although rangefinder-coupled with close focusing down to 0.7 meters (2.3 feet), the lens can focus as close as 0.3 meters (0.98 feet) when used in live view or adapted. Brightin Star notes that 100 degrees of focus throw covers infinity to 0.7 meters, while an additional 207 degrees covers the relatively narrow distance from 0.3 to 0.7 meters. That 307 degrees of total focus rotation is quite a lot, and Brightin Star describes it as “cinema style.”.

Industry observers note that the 35mm f/1.7 prime is a compact, relatively lightweight lens. It measures just 43 millimeters (1.7 inches) long and weighs around 260 grams (9.2 ounces). It accepts 39mm front filters. Part of Brightin Star’s new “Apex” series of lenses, the 35mm f/1.7 APO ASPH. promises precision build quality and high-end optical performance.

“We believe a truly exceptional M-mount lens should never have to choose between heritage and innovation,” Brightin Star says. “The Apex Series was created with this belief at its core. It preserves the timeless, understated character of classic M lenses while bringing together advanced optics, precision mechanics, and uncompromising standards of craftsmanship.”.

On the topic of image quality, the lens features 11 elements arranged across seven groups. There are some notable elements inside, including three double-sided aspherical lenses, three high-refractive pieces of glass, and an ED element. There are also two floating lens groups that move independently during focusing, which the manufacturer says better controls distance-related aberrations and reduces spherical aberrations at close range. The lens also promises minimized focus breathing.

As evidenced by the “APO” in its name, Brightin Star says this is an “apochromatic” lens. While there’s no precise, industry-standard definition for what level of performance that requires, Brightin Star promises minimal chromatic aberration. An apochromatic lens focuses red, blue, and green wavelengths of light at the exact same point on the image plane. The closer a lens gets to achieving this ideal, the fewer chromatic aberrations it exhibits, all else being equal.

According to recent reports, the Brightin Star MF 35mm f/1.7 APO ASPH. lens is available now for $1,099 for Leica M. An adapter adds $30, pushing the price to $1,129.

#148930. Preserving Henry Ford’s failed Amazonian empire

Preserving Henry Ford’s failed Amazonian empire

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1224 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Deep in the Amazon Rainforest, in the Brazilian state of Pará, lies the dilapidated settlement of Fordlândia.
  • It has been revealed that earlier this year, almost a century after Fordlândia was built, a federal court ruled that it must be protected as a heritage site under the Brazilian constitution.
  • It has been revealed that ford’s company originally acquired the land for what would become Fordlândia in 1927.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Deep in the Amazon Rainforest, in the Brazilian state of Pará, lies the dilapidated settlement of Fordlândia. A once bustling—albeit highly exploitative—village, it was established by the US industrialist Henry Ford in the 1920s. Fordlândia’s sole purpose was to serve as a rubber-tapping enterprise that would provide materials for the Ford Motor Manufacturer. But less than a decade after its founding, the rubber crops failed. With the development of synthetic rubber following close behind, Ford abandoned the project in 1945, and the village along the Tapajós River fell into severe disrepair.

It has been revealed that earlier this year, almost a century after Fordlândia was built, a federal court ruled that it must be protected as a heritage site under the Brazilian constitution. Local and national authorities have until the end of this month to come up with a conservation proposal.

It has been revealed that ford’s company originally acquired the land for what would become Fordlândia in 1927. He envisioned building a Midwestern-style village as a hub for latex extraction, supplying materials for his factories in Michigan. Ford hoped to upend the dominance of British-controlled rubber plantations in Southeast Asia, which had left US manufacturers dependent on foreign suppliers.

Fordlândia, beyond giving the Ford Motor Firm control over its supply of raw materials, was imagined as a self-sufficient settlement for around 10,000 people in the Amazon. Ford himself viewed Fordlândia as a sociological experiment intended to “Americanise” the local population, although the tycoon never visited his dystopian village. Workers there, many of them Indigenous people and migrants from northeastern Brazil, endured cultural subjugation and often faced dangerous conditions—including having to work through the hottest part of the day. Hundreds of people died during the short-lived project.

It has been revealed that workers organised a mutiny in 1930 after unreasonable restrictions were imposed in Fordlândia, including the prohibition of alcohol and tobacco, as well as the requirement of US customs like square dancing and a diet of wholewheat bread, brown rice, oatmeal and canned peaches. Shortly afterwards there was a full-scale riot, in which workers chased their American managers and the village cook into the jungle. The Brazilian army was brought in to restore order. The company subsequently fired a number of workers and appointed a latest manager to complete Fordlândia’s infrastructure. (An agreement on serving different food to the workers was also reached.).

Fordlândia Dance Hall, around 1933 The Collections of the Henry Ford.

Industry observers note that ford’s social experiment unfolded alongside agricultural problems. Without the consultation of local experts, the rubber trees had been planted too close together. This made them vulnerable to disease and pests, and the growing conditions along the river were unsuitable. In 1933, at the recommendation of the American plant pathologist James Robert Weir, a second plantation was established downstream at Belterra, where conditions were more appropriate. Although it fared better than Fordlândia, production remained costly and it never became commercially viable.

Industry observers note that no usable latex was ever produced in Fordlândia. After investing millions of dollars with no return, Ford sold the land back to the Brazilian government. The population dropped by more than 90% in the following years, but squatters and families moved back into the decaying structures in the 2000s. Around 3,000 people live in Fordlândia today, even as the village remains unconnected to paved roads.

Industry observers note that the federal process for the designation of Fordlândia as a heritage site has been unresolved since the 1990s, when the move was first suggested by local advocates. In 2015, Brazil’s federal public prosecutor’s office filed a lawsuit stating that the site had “unquestionable” cultural value. In 2024, the National Institute of Historic and Artistic Heritage (Iphan) countered that Fordlândia lacked the criteria required for federal heritage listing, pointing to the loss of its original characteristics and the site’s deteriorated condition.

But in May 2026 a federal court ruled that, even without formal heritage status, the site should be protected. This decision was based on a 1988 constitutional article that mandates the conservation of both material and immaterial assets connected to Brazilian communities. The court added that uncertainty over ownership of the site had been used repeatedly as justification for inaction, and that the state of Pará and the municipality of Aveiro (which administers Fordlândia) had previously signed an agreement to begin conservation measures that never materialised. It also alleged that some interventions had been carried out without authorisation.

A Fordlândia sawmill in 1931, before the Ford Motor Company’s rubber-plantation project was halted The Collections of the Henry Ford.

The court ruled that Iphan must now work with the state and municipality to deliver a plan by the end of November 2026, outlining the responsibilities of each government entity and the needs of each site in Fordlândia—including emergency measures for structures at imminent risk. Once approved, conservation work must begin within 30 days. If deadlines are not met, the court will impose a daily fine of $2,000 (10,000 reais) on the federal government and Iphan, and a $1,000 (5,000 reais) fine on the state and municipality. Iphan must also begin the administrative process to recognise Fordlândia as a heritage site.

In a recent development, in a statement to The Art Newspaper, a spokesperson for Iphan says the agency does not comment on ongoing legal proceedings. It remains unclear if Iphan aims to counter the court’s decision. “In May 2024, Iphan’s cultural-heritage advisory council denied Fordlândia’s designation as Brazilian cultural heritage,” the spokesperson says. “Iphan reiterates that it remains committed to the preservation of Brazilian cultural heritage, as mandated by the constitution.”.

Sources indicate that the sites to be reviewed include the former Fordlândia Hospital, designed by the Detroit architect Albert Kahn; the long-abandoned industrial and port warehouses; the houses of the American Village, where the tech giant’s American managers lived; the workers’ village; the Henry Ford School; the Cine Patinha, a cinema whose roof has recently collapsed; and a convent on a cliff overlooking the Tapajós River, built in the post-Ford era and active until the early 2010s. All these structures have been exposed to the Amazon’s heat, humidity and heavy rainfall for years.

Fordlândia remains highly remote, receiving few outside visitors and requiring a minimum six-hour trip to reach via high-speed boat. Still, there is evidence that intrepid travellers have made the journey. A manufacturer specialising in tours of the Amazon is at the moment offering a five-day visit to the region, including a stop in Fordlândia, for approximately $3,000 (16,000 reais) per person. Reviews for “Fordlândia Ghost Town” on TripAdvisor average 4.7 out of 5 stars, with one reviewer in 2016 calling the site “historical, magical and melancholic”, and another saying it tells a story of “hubris, determination, paternalism and ultimately failure”.

According to recent reports, although Fordlândia is unlikely to be commercialised as a tourist destination, the village’s surviving infrastructure has come to represent an unusual and failed attempt to Americanise and industrialise the Amazon. The remnants of the settlement also tell the story of the Brazilian workers who lived there, and those who have continued to inhabit it. The Brazilian government maintains that Fordlândia has “unquestionable historical, cultural and architectural value”, and that it represents “an American attempt to break the British monopoly on rubber and bring modern infrastructure to the middle of the Amazon”.

The world’s leading architects and designers from over 40 countries joined to celebrate Dezeen Awards 2026, in partnership with Trimble, announcing this year’s winners at a party in London.

More than 550 guests from countries including Angola, Canada and India, as well as Japan, South Africa and Uruguay, joined Dezeen for the event at the historic Royal Opera House in central London.

Guests were welcomed with a champagne reception provided by exclusive drinks partner Veuve Clicquot as they entered the Grade-II listed Paul Hamlyn Hall at the opera house.

The hall’s glazed interior was illuminated and washed in vivid colours drawn from this year’s awards graphic identity in a show design led by Hingston Studio.

Partygoers enjoyed their drinks set against a textile softwall bar backdrop designed by Stephanie Forsythe and Todd MacAllen for Canadian studio Molo, known for its sculptural space partitions, furniture and lighting made from paper and textile.

Industry observers note that dezeen’s co-CEOs Benedict Hobson and Wai Shin Li opened the evening’s ceremony. They welcomed Dezeen’s founding director and board member Rupinder Bhogal to the stage to lead a tribute to the magazine’s founder, the late Marcus Fairs, in honour of its 20th year.

After guests joined in a toast, Hobson and Li then introduced the evening’s keynote speaker, Norman Foster.

Sources indicate that the British architect delivered a speech that explored creative and artificial intelligence within the evolving landscape of global architecture. Drawing on his prolific career, the nonagenarian advocated that meaningful innovation requires challenging the status quo.

Dezeen’s editorial director of special projects Max Fraser and awards and events director Claire Barrett then led the evening’s winner announcements.

First to be announced were the design categories, which saw design project of the year awarded to the V&A East’s wayfinding scheme.

Stockholm-based Simon Skinner and British-Nigerian designer Yinka Ilori were named as this year’s emerging designer of the year and designer of the year, respectively.

Skinner and Ilori won in this year’s Designers of the Year initiative, which recognises the best emerging and established talent whose innovative work has made a notable impact on the industry across architecture, interiors and design.

In a recent development, interiors project of the year, sponsored by Gaggenau, went to Barcelona-based Raul Sanchez’s renovation of an old sailor’s home. Australian designer Yasmine Ghoniem was awarded emerging interior designer of the year, with Tokyo-based Keiji Ashizawa taking the award as this year’s established designer. The interiors project categories were also sponsored by Programa and Framery.

Architecture project of the year was awarded to Daichi’s treetop sauna. The architecture project categories were also sponsored by Michelmersh and Sanderson.

The evening’s presentations culminated with Japanese architect Shohei Kuma and French‑Spanish architect Elsa Escobedo jointly winning emerging architect of the year, while world-renowned practitioner Lina Ghotmeh was named architect of the year.

All the winners received a bespoke trophy made from sustainably harvested cork produced by Portuguese manufacturer Corticeira Amorim.

Dezeen Awards winners, VIPs and invited guests continued celebrating into the early hours at an exclusive afterparty sponsored by creative technology studio Made by On at the House of Louie‘s sequestered cocktail hideaway, the Alligator Bar.

All Dezeen Awards 2026 winners were published on Dezeen last Monday evening. Each winner was also featured on a dedicated page on the awards website.

The photography is by Iona Wolff and Olivia Chenery.

Sources indicate that dezeen Awards 2026 in partnership with TrimbleDezeen Awards is the ultimate accolade for architects and designers worldwide. The ninth edition of the annual awards is in partnership with global technology tech giant Trimble. Through connected hardware and software solutions, Trimble helps designers to transform the way they shape spaces and buildings as well as drive productivity in the process. Trimble’s collaboration with Dezeen Awards demonstrates its ongoing commitment to inspiring and supporting creative excellence across the globe.

Tech Report: AI-Generated Characters Are Stealing Content Creators’ Viral Videos

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Content creators are increasingly discovering AI-generated versions of their videos in which almost everything is identical, except that they have been replaced by AI-generated characters.
  • From musicians and chefs to comedians, content creators are finding their performances copied by AI-generated characters that mimic their movements, jokes, and even the backgrounds in their original videos.
  • In a recent development, the phenomenon, known as “reskinning,” is becoming increasingly common across social media thanks to cheap and accessible AI tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Content creators are increasingly discovering AI-generated versions of their videos in which almost everything is identical, except that they have been replaced by AI-generated characters.

From musicians and chefs to comedians, content creators are finding their performances copied by AI-generated characters that mimic their movements, jokes, and even the backgrounds in their original videos.

In a recent development, the phenomenon, known as “reskinning,” is becoming increasingly common across social media thanks to cheap and accessible AI tools. People can take an existing video and replace the original performer with an artificial character, often designed to look funny, realistic, or hypersexualized.

According to recent reports, the Instagram page More Perfect Union points to Higgsfield AI and its new Genjutsu tool that allows users to upload any video file and remix it with the user’s own character, locations, or product. However, other elements of the video remain untouched.

Sources indicate that just a few weeks ago, Nvidia invested in Higgsfield AI in a Series B funding round that raised $400 million. It gave Higgsfield a valuation of $5.4 billion.

A post shared by More Perfect Union (@perfectunion).

Sources indicate that sophie Lloyd, a U.K.-based guitarist who tours with U.S. rapper Machine Gun Kelly, tells the BBC she has spent years building an online following, only to see AI accounts reproduce content created by musicians and other performers.

“A lot [of these accounts] are getting thousands of views, thousands of followers, just for literally doing nothing and stealing the stuff that we’ve created,” Lloyd states.

Dr. Tina Kendall, an expert in online culture at Anglia Ruskin University, tells the British broadcaster that the practice is often less about experimentation with AI and more about exploiting content that has already demonstrated its popularity.

“What these tools allow people to do is just automatically take a viral concept that’s already existing and to reuse it through these reskinning tools,” she notes.

While some accounts may use the technology for entertainment, Kendall says others are deliberately copying successful videos in the hope of attracting an audience and generating revenue.

She sees the trend as part of a wider online “hustle culture,” in which accounts look to turn attention and engagement into money. That can mean directing followers toward subscription-based fan pages featuring adult content, promoting risky cryptocurrency products such as meme coins, or simply taking advantage of monetization features offered by social media platforms.

For the original creators, identifying and stopping the accounts responsible can be extremely difficult.

Alwyn Cruz, who has built a following on social media by exposing AI-generated musicians, describes trying to shut down these accounts as a game of whack-a-mole.

According to recent reports, “You don’t even know who’s making these [videos]. And then if you shut it down, they’re just going to create another,” he says.

Cruz says the problem extends well beyond musicians, with performers from a variety of disciplines finding their work replicated.

“It’s not only guitarists that are being cloned: there are drummers, taekwondo players that are being cloned, and I’ve seen this all over the internet.”.

The accessibility of AI reskinning tools like Higgsfield means the practice could become increasingly difficult to contain. Creators can spend years developing an online presence and refining a style that audiences recognize, only to find that the same performances can be reproduced with a different face and a few clicks.

And while the AI-generated versions may be attracting attention, the people behind the original performances are often left watching someone else benefit from their work.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Roboto Studio rebuilt the Flowhub brand identity around one mark, Helvetica Now and Neon Moss green, from the website to the checkout screen.

It has been revealed that flowhub runs point of sale, payments, ecommerce, marketing and reporting for specialty retailers across the United States, from cannabis dispensaries to liquor stores and CBD shops. More than $4B in sales passes through it every year. Its old purple identity is gone. In its place, Roboto Studio built a system on a single mark, one typeface and one bright green, then carried the same parts into the website and the product interface, so the homepage, the dashboard and the payment screen at the counter are made from the same pieces. The line that runs through it all says it plainly: Retail moves fast. We move faster.

Helvetica Now does the talking. Display Bold carries the headlines at sizes that fill the frame, white on Rich Black, while Display Medium, Text Medium and Text Regular step down through the interface without changing voice. The specimen page lines the weights up beside a full character set, and the restraint shows in how little else the layouts need. The mark is a compact flowing form that reads at a glance and crops into a poster motif at bus stop scale. On the homepage the grid keeps real product screens in view, a strip of retailer logos leading into the hardware and apps, Maui OS, ecommerce, kiosk and delivery, each shown as the actual screen.

Recent findings suggest that two materials carry the system. Liquid chrome gives the mark its weight, a molten rendering that turns up on the poster, the SOC 2 shield and the map of backers. Frosted glass does the quieter work, layering the interface panels, the one platform stack and the deal cards Max drafts over photography. Color stays disciplined. Pearly White and Rich Black cover most of every surface, Pearl holds the panels, Neon Moss appears only on the one action that matters, and Sunburst orange is kept for anything that needs attention. The Intelligence dashboard opens on what needs attention today, sales, margin and stock value at the top, with Max drafting a reorder before a bestseller runs out. At the counter, the payment screen turns fully Neon Moss with a single word, Paid, large enough to read from the customer side.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by José Hevia.

Spanish studio Raúl Sánchez Architects turned a former washhouse into Casa de las Lavanderas, with a lightwell that is a “modern translation of the old wells” used by local laundry workers.

The home is located on Barcelona’s picturesque Calle Aiguafreda street, historically an area where washerwomen used wells to handwash their clients’ clothes.

Raúl Sánchez Architects, which won interiors project of the year at this year’s Dezeen Awards, turned one of the old laundry houses on the street into the two-storey Casa de las Lavanderas.

The house is now home to a couple and their newborn baby.

The lower level of the 80-square-metre building was partly underground and very dark, leading the studio to look for fresh solutions to add more light.

“Since the ground floor is semi-basement, the area furthest from Aiguafreda Street was darker, so to bring light into it, I incorporated this lightwell topped with a skylight,” studio founder Rául Sánchez told Dezeen.

The lightwell also functions as a “modern translation of the old wells” that used to provide water for the laundry workers.

Casa de las Lavanderas faces two streets – Calle Aiguafreda and Calle Granollers – and has entrances on both sides, with the Calle Aiguafreda entrance sitting 1.5 metres lower than that on Calle Granollers.

From here, one flight of stairs leads down to the lower level and the Calle Aiguafreda entrance, and another up to the house’s upper level.

The 40-square-metre lower level houses an open-proposal living, dining and kitchen area, a bathroom and a small study.

This can be partitioned off from the living space using folding doors made from wood and rice paper, inspired by the clients’ time living in Japan.

In the kitchen, Sánchez mentioned he added a mirror-clad island to “introduce a sense of fragility without disrupting the open feel of the space”.

The upper level, meanwhile, houses the home’s bedrooms and a bathroom. The two floors are connected by the Klein-blue lightwell, which has oculi on all four sides to help distribute the illumination from its skylight throughout the space.

Sánchez wanted to “bring that picturesque atmosphere of Aiguafreda Street into the house, making it part of its surroundings by reclaiming that well – now translated into a lightwell that also helps regulate the home’s temperature.”.

This was one of many tailor-made solutions to turn the former laundry house into a home.

“There were many challenges, both technical – access to the mezzanine level, the fresh staircase, the structural reinforcements – and functional, like fitting the program into just 80 square metres,” Sánchez said.

His studio also worked with materials that would complement the existing ones, using terracotta tiles on the ground floor to extend the traditional exterior clay paving and adding colored glazed tiles to the washbasins and bathroom walls.

“Ultimately, the goal is always to create a cohesive, overarching project that addresses all these challenges and offers something extra – something almost hard to put into words, but that translates into simply feeling good in the space,” Sánchez concluded.

Rául Sánchez Architects is right now working on the final phase of the project, the design of its orchard and garden, which will begin at the start of 2027.

The studio also recently designed a concrete home with a sunken courtyard in Cala Tamarit.

Architecture team: Nerea Moya, Marta Gámiz, FlaviaStructure consultant: Diagonal EstructurasEngineering consultant: Mares Engyniers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A family photographer has been arrested for allegedly hiding income from her photography business to obtain more than $30,000 in food assistance benefits.

Mary Miller, a 31-year-old Wisconsin-based family photographer who operated under the name Fawn Focus Photography, is facing multiple charges related to public assistance fraud.

According to a long-term investigation by the Dodge County Sheriff’s Office in Juneau, Wisconsin, Miller allegedly failed to report her earnings as a self-employed photographer while claiming FoodShare and childcare assistance benefits over several years. FoodShare is Wisconsin’s food assistance program for individuals and families with limited incomes.

According to a report by Fox 11 News, an investigation was launched after Dodge County Economic Support uncovered apparent inconsistencies between Miller’s tax records, employment records, court documents, and applications for public assistance.

Authorities allege that the photographer provided inaccurate information about her income and residency when applying for benefits, including failing to disclose earnings from her business Fawn Focus Photography.

Industry observers note that between 2019 and 2025, Miller allegedly received more than $30,000 in FoodShare benefits that she was not entitled to claim. She also received more than $22,000 in childcare assistance benefits, although investigators were still determining how much of that funding was improperly obtained.

According to online court records, Miller faces six counts of failing to disclose an event affecting her eligibility for benefits and six counts of failing to report the receipt of income or assets. The photographer made her initial court appearance this month and was issued a $5,000 signature bond.

It has been revealed that “Public assistance programs exist to help individuals and families during times of genuine need and are funded by hardworking taxpayers,” Dodge County Sheriff Dale J. Schmidt tells Fox 11 News in a statement. “When someone is alleged to have concealed income or provided false information in order to obtain benefits, it undermines public trust and diverts limited resources away from those who legitimately qualify for assistance.”.

Previously, PetaPixel reported on a photographer who was sentenced to five years in federal prison for defrauding a family out of $4.6 million and using $200,000 of the money to purchase Taylor Swift concert tickets. 46-year-old photographer Chanise Coyne was given jail time after pleading guilty to wire fraud over a multimillion-dollar fraud scheme involving fictional child modeling events.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has now been five straight quarters of growth for the transformed, resurgent Eastman Kodak.

After facing immense financial challenges for decades, including warnings about its ability to continue as a “going concern” last year, Eastman Kodak has risen from the ashes like a phoenix, cashing in on analog’s revival.

According to recent reports, the star of the show for the Rochester, New York-based Kodak is its Advanced Materials and Chemicals (AM&C) division, which posted 21% revenue growth in Q3 2026 compared to Q3 2025. While AM&C’s $99 million in revenue is significantly less than Kodak’s $165 million in Print revenue, the Print division’s revenue actually dipped 7% year-over-year. In total, Kodak’s consolidated revenues of $276 million this past quarter are up 3%. Profits are up, too, increasing by 7%.

“Kodak delivered strong performance in the third quarter, once again achieving year-over-year improvement in revenue, gross profit and Operational EBITDA,” indicates Jim Continenza, Kodak’s Executive Chairman and CEO, in SEC filings.

Recent findings suggest that “We continue to execute our long-term strategy and are seeing a return on our ongoing investments. Our primary growth engine, AM&C, is now our fastest-growing, most profitable unit. Our print business has performed well for the year to date despite challenging economic conditions. And, most importantly, we generated $27 million in cash for Q3, an important indicator of the operational strength of our business. Looking forward, we’re focused on continuing to invest in our core businesses and finishing the year with profitable growth,” Continenza continues.

Sources indicate that as Continenza indicates, AM&C is Eastman Kodak’s fastest-growing and most profitable business unit. What exactly is AM&C, though? Kodak says AM&C covers the manufacturing of still, motion picture, and industrial films, plus specialty chemicals related to film, technologies, and medicine.

As CineD reports, in a call with investors, Continenza specifically called out the growing desire among Hollywood filmmakers to shoot their biggest projects on film.

“Film continues to be the capture medium of choice for major features,” Continenza told investors.

It has been revealed that while Christopher Nolan’s record-breaking IMAX epic, The Odyssey, made a lot of headlines for its use of over two million feet of film, it is just one example of the return of film to Hollywood. Kodak had a great story about The Odyssey in August that dug a bit deeper into the movie’s use of Kodak film.

Kodak states award-winning cinematographer and Director of Photography Hoyte van Hoytema used Kodak Vision3 250D 5207 for daytime exteriors and bright interiors, and Kodak Vision3 500T 5219 for low-light and night scenes.

“The 250D and 500T are my sweet spot filmstocks. I love their grain structures and they’re very much my functional workhorses. The way I work with lenses, NDs, daylight and lights for night scenes, falls within the sensitivity curves of both those stocks. They are both versatile too. For example, I can shoot a little bit longer into magic hour with the 250D and I don’t have to resort too quickly into going higher-up in ASA,” van Hoytema told Kodak.

Earlier this year, Kodak celebrated seven movies shot on Kodak that competed for the Palme d’Or at Cannes 2026, and the legendary film tech giant routinely updates its list of productions shot on film.

Paper Tiger, Disclosure Day, and Marty Supreme are just a few significant names on the list. Continenza also mentioned Sense and Sensibility and Digger in his call.

In a recent development, then, of course, there’s Eastman Kodak’s growing still film business. Over the past year-plus, Eastman Kodak has brought photographic film sales back under its purview, rebranding many different stocks and even unveiling some newly introduced, albeit familiar, ones. The organization reintroduced some larger-format photo film stocks a few months ago, too.

Between Hollywood’s reignited love affair with film and Eastman Kodak’s investment in both motion picture and still film production, it’s immediately evident that Eastman Kodak believes its path to future success goes through analog. The licensing deals for smash hit Kodak-branded products don’t hurt, either.

  • It has been revealed that “The intended use of this list is unclear,” Bunch wrote of “The Smithsonian Institution Renewal Proposal” that the staffer was seen editing on his laptop on a crowded train in late October.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that lonnie G. Bunch III, the outgoing leader of the Smithsonian Institution, sent a letter to staff on Tuesday (24 November) in an attempt to quell fears of a political takeover after photos leaked of a Trump aide working on an overhaul blueprint while riding the city's metro.

It has been revealed that “The intended use of this list is unclear,” Bunch wrote of “The Smithsonian Institution Renewal Proposal” that the staffer was seen editing on his laptop on a crowded train in late October. “What remains clear is that the Smithsonian is an independent institution with the responsibility and privilege to present accurate information to millions of visitors through our scholarship and educational programmes.”.

Recent findings suggest that photos of the staffer working on the proposal—in full view of fellow passengers on public transit—had been published by ProPublica the previous day (23 November). Formatted as a 25-item to-do list, the draft focused largely on the beleaguered National Museum of American History (NMAH), a recent focal point in the White House’s attempts to rewrite US history.

The list included firing NMAH’s director and a dozen other administrators and curators, opening a upcoming permanent exhibition centred on “Western civilisation inheritance”, erecting a new “colossus statue” of George Washington for NMAH’s entrance and overhauling its online curriculum for schoolchildren to “realign educational materials with patriotism, not ideology”. The blueprint also called for a review of Smithsonian grants to “woke third parties” like the American Alliance of Museums.

The Washington Metro’s Smithsonian station Photo: GeneralPunger, via Wikimedia Commons.

Given that it was in process prior to the midterm elections—which resulted in a landslide for Democrats, who gained a majority in both houses of congress—it remains unclear if this plan for the Smithsonian is still in the works. However, congressional Democrats are ready to fight.

“I intend to investigate these matters in the 120th congress and vigorously defend the Smithsonian’s independence,” Chellie Pingree, the ranking member of the congressional subcommittee that funds the Smithsonian, wrote in a letter to the institution’s Board of Regents after the ProPublica leak. “This reporting is extremely concerning, but not surprising given this administration’s previous attempts to illegally impound Smithsonian Institution-appropriated funding, use federal agencies to spread misinformation about the Smithsonian, and release a demonstrably false report accusing the Smithsonian Institution of systemic bias in its curatorial decisions.”.

US President Donald Trump has been steadily attacking the Smithsonian ever since he took office for his second term, with a goal of realigning the institution to complement his own political agenda. Last year, Trump attempted to fire the director of the National Portrait Gallery, Kim Sajet, over her support for diversity, equity and inclusion programmes. She later resigned and now heads the Milwaukee Art Museum in Wisconsin.

It has been revealed that in July, NMAH director Anthea M. Hartig was summoned to appear before congress and interrogated by Republican lawmakers after a White House report concluded the museum was not “proudly patriotic” with leadership having “denigrated and displaced whites, males, Christians and Americans”. A few days later, Trump ordered that signs be placed outside the NMAH, warning visitors of "ideological capture" and "inaccurate information" inside. (The signs have yet to be erected.).

#148921. Breaking: YouTube Is Suddenly Obsessed With Views

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (853 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Petapixel ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: YouTube Is Suddenly Obsessed With Views

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (853 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This year, YouTube has changed how it counts views twice — and both occurred within three months of each other, which is shifting the paradigm of expectations for creators and advertisers.
  • The first adjustment came back in August when YouTube changed when it would count a view, separating the metric into two parts: a standard view as well as an engaged view.
  • Recent findings suggest that “A view is now defined as counting from the very first frame — whether that’s a Short appearing in the feed or a long-form video autoplaying on the Home page,” YouTube explains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This year, YouTube has changed how it counts views twice — and both occurred within three months of each other, which is shifting the paradigm of expectations for creators and advertisers. It also appears both creepy and desperate on YouTube’s part.

The first adjustment came back in August when YouTube changed when it would count a view, separating the metric into two parts: a standard view as well as an engaged view.

Recent findings suggest that “A view is now defined as counting from the very first frame — whether that’s a Short appearing in the feed or a long-form video autoplaying on the Home page,” YouTube explains. “An engaged view is defined as clicking to watch or watching past the initial seconds. This has been, and will continue to be, how you qualify to earn (as long as the content is also public).”.

That engaged view is basically what standard, public views were before the change and remains in place because YouTube wanted to make its view numbers appear larger to the public, but it also didn’t want to have to tie creator payouts to those higher numbers. Basically, YouTube wanted to have its cake and eat it, too.

In a recent development, youTube indicates it changed the way it counts public views because it wanted to standardize metrics across formats and therefore measure audience reach more accurately. In short, because Meta and TikTok count views instantly on short-form content, YouTube felt like its view numbers on long-form content weren’t keeping up with the times.

This does, at least from YouTube’s perspective, make sense. Short-form has become a huge part of how people consume content now, for better or for worse. While YouTube Shorts are not nearly as popular as Instagram Reels or TikTok, YouTube does have them, and separating how it counted views there to be in line with the competition without adjusting them on long-form felt disjointed.

It’s the second view change YouTube made in 2026 that feels, as I stated at the top, particularly creepy and desperate. Starting earlier this month, YouTube started estimating how many people are in the room with a viewer when they play a video on a television and counting those estimations toward the public view count.

Sources indicate that “TVs are usually shared devices where friends, families, and communities come together to watch their favorite content. Until now, one TV playback has only counted as a single public view, even if several people watched together on the same living room screen. By updating public view counts to include co-views, we’re solving this measurement gap, better aligning with long-standing TV industry standards, and telling a more accurate story of how viewers watch your content,” YouTube says.

In a recent development, when first hearing how YouTube is approaching this, it sounds like YouTube is finding some way to actually see into living rooms. YouTube says this isn’t the case and it doesn’t actually know how many people are sitting in front of the television. Instead, it uses a video’s genre, audience demographics, and the time of day to guess. If YouTube thinks the video attracts a group and it is being watched in the evening, it will use that data to estimate more than one viewer.

“Co-view rate works as a ratio to show how estimated co-views contribute to your overall public views. For example, a Co-view rate of 1.10 means that for every 1,100 views of a video on TV, 1,000 are primary views from the device playback and 100 come from co-viewing,” YouTube explains.

Okay, sure, but why? It just seems like YouTube is obsessed with increasing its view counts to pump up how the platform is perceived while simultaneously not giving creators anything newly introduced. None of these changes actually affect revenue for YouTubers.

“This change only updates public view counts. Your actual creator earnings, ad revenue splits, and YouTube Partner Program (YPP) requirements remain unchanged,” YouTube stipulates regarding co-views.

In a recent development, that’s the part that really stands out. Sure, not giving more revenue based on the newly introduced calculation of a standard view from August makes sense. That’s not an additional person or viewer more than before; it’s just a new way of deciding at what point the view starts. Fine.

But if co-views are calculating additional people, there is no reason why those views shouldn’t count toward earned revenue. Those are, factually, additional human eyes seeing those videos.

Instead, YouTube gets to pitch advertisers on massive living-room reach while paying creators strictly on single-device clicks. Until those estimated eyeballs translate into actual ad revenue, co-views feel less like a win for creators and more like creative accounting designed to make YouTube look bigger than it is.

I guess when investors are demanding constant growth and the number of humans whose eyes can actually watch content does eventually reach a finite point, the only option is to just make up more eyes.
